description_full: Martin Marietta Materials, Inc., a natural resource-based building materials company, supplies aggregates and heavy-side building materials to the construction industry in the United States and internationally. It operates through East Group and West Group segments. The company offers crushed stone, sand, and gravel products; ready mixed concrete and asphalt; and paving products and services for use in the infrastructure projects, and nonresidential and residential construction projects, as well as in the railroad, agricultural, utility, and environmental industries. It also produces magnesia-based chemicals products, and dolomitic lime primarily to customers for steel production and soil stabilization. Its chemical products are used in flame retardants, wastewater treatment, pulp and paper production, and other applications. The company was founded in 1939 and is based in Raleigh, North Carolina.

financial_summary: Martin Marietta Materials, Inc. is a large-cap basic materials business with a $36.5B market cap on $6.2B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -0% over the past three years and +6% annually across the full decade — essentially flat, and a business treading water is rarely a path to compounding.

Returns on capital run at 8% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, and 23% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $978M in free cash flow — roughly 16 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.57× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.5× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 6.2×.

Shareholder yield is only 1.8%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 16% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 1.8× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

Trade policy and tariff whiplash — materials producers are first-order casualties of protectionist swings, and margin gets squeezed from both input and output pricing.

sect: Its 23% operating margin runs 14pp above the Basic Materials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 1.79x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 0.4% of sector revenue and 0.7% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-2.3% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 221 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a steep downtrend, down 21% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 28% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 30% and a beta of 0.91, it moves roughly with the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $396.1M traded a day, and interest is running hot at 1.6x its yearly average volume.
In past sell-offs it fell 48% in the 2020 crash, 33% in the 2022 bear market and 52% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $191 (margin of safety -169%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 42%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $144 to $251 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Basic Materials peers: P/E 38.3 vs 16.3, EV/EBITDA 22.4 vs 8.3 and P/FCF 37.3 vs 22.4 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 19% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 2.7% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 2.9% (vs the 8% bar).
The 24 covering analysts target $627 on average, 22% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 8% falls short of the cost of capital of 8.5%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.36).
It runs a 23% gross margin and converts 16% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 1.57x.
ROE of 11% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.9x equity multiplier).
It spends 0.7% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 2.5x net debt to EBITDA ($67.0M of cash against $5.3B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 6.2x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 3.7, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at -0.1% over 3 years, 5.4% over 5 years and 5.7% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
At current returns, reinvesting 81% of profits supports about 6.6% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 7.2% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 0.98 and a backlog worth 3% of annual revenue.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.3x, 13.1% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 21, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own 16.1%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 85%.
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.8% (1.2% in buybacks and 0.7% in dividends).
The share count has grown 2.7% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
It has paid a dividend for 31 consecutive years, raising it 7.0% a year over the last five.
people: With about 9,600 employees, each generates about $641K of revenue, in line with the Basic Materials median, and revenue has grown 8.6% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $102K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $4.2M (7x revenue per employee).
